title: ImageNet-trained CNNs are not biased towards texture: Revisiting feature re

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5.2, Medical Imaging paragraph versus Figure 4 legend/caption
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The MI plot legend lists BloodMNIST, BreastMNIST, DermaMNIST, OCTMNIST, and PathMNIST. However, the text discusses results for RetinaMNIST and ChestMNIST: "texture suppression yields ... relatively little effect in RetinaMNIST and DermaMNIST" and "except in ChestMNIST." RetinaMNIST and ChestMNIST are not among the five datasets represented in Figure 4, while BreastMNIST and OCTMNIST are not discussed. Thus the prose cannot describe the plotted experiment as claimed.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5.2, Remote Sensing paragraph and Figure 4 caption versus Figure 4 legend
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Figure 4 RS legend identifies AID, EuroSAT, NWPU, RESISC45, and UC Merced. In contrast, both the caption and the RS paragraph say the experiment used "UCMerced, RSD46-WHU, DeepGlobe, PatternNet, and AID." Only AID and UC Merced overlap. The reported curves therefore have irreconcilable dataset identities, invalidating the associated domain-level interpretation until corrected.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5.1, Experimental Setup: construction of the "ImageNet16-like" dataset
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The manuscript says the dataset was made by "selecting 50 images per category," but immediately says that "Categories with fewer confident predictions were left as is, leading to class imbalance." Selecting 50 images per category produces a balanced sample unless categories/images were subsequently excluded; no exclusion rule, confidence threshold, model used to determine confidence, final category counts, or category identities is supplied. This is both internally inconsistent and prevents reproduction of the central human/model experiment.

Humans classify through an interface with 16 categories, whereas models are said to use "the argmax class across all subclasses." The manuscript does not define the 16 categories, the mapping from ImageNet's 1,000 synsets/subclasses to those categories, or how predictions outside the 16-category response space are scored. Without an explicitly common label space and aggregation/scoring rule, the reported human-model accuracy comparison is not interpretable or reproducible.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract; Sections 5.1 and 6: conclusion that CNNs are not texture-biased and instead rely more on local shape
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The conclusion compares accuracy losses induced by non-equivalent corruptions as though they measured commensurate amounts of feature removal. The paper's own Table 2 shows bilateral filtering leaves substantial texture metrics intact (LV 0.548 and HFE 0.493 relative to the original), while patch shuffle produces maximal LV/HFE (1.000) and very low edge-structure scores (ESSIM 0.205 and GC 0.147), as well as conspicuous artificial patch boundaries. Therefore a larger accuracy loss under patch shuffle cannot establish greater reliance on shape than texture; it may result from much stronger distribution shift, artifact sensitivity, and incomplete texture suppression. The stated limitations acknowledge these issues but do not support the categorical headline claim of "no evidence" for texture bias.

The cross-domain attribution is confounded by training initialization. Figure 4 evaluates CV models pretrained on ImageNet and then fine-tuned, but evaluates MI and RS models from scratch: "Top row ... pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tuned on CV datasets" versus "Middle row ... trained from scratch" and "Bottom row ... trained from scratch." Nevertheless, the paper attributes the differences to domain properties, e.g., "CV models are most reliant on local shape," "MI models exhibit stronger dependence on color," and "RS models exhibit the highest texture reliance." Pretraining is explicitly acknowledged elsewhere as affecting robustness, so this design cannot isolate domain effects.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4 and Table 1: Channel Shuffle as a color-suppression transformation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states that "Channel Shuffle disrupts color correlations without altering intensity." A conventional RGB channel shuffle is a permutation of the R, G, and B channels. Such a permutation preserves the joint channel information and pairwise correlations up to relabeling; it does not suppress chromatic information, and it generally changes color appearance. If a different operation was intended, it is not defined. Consequently it cannot be presented as a validated complementary color-suppression method.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1/Table 2: claimed validation of all feature-suppression transformations
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The framework claims to validate transformations that suppress shape, texture, and color. Table 2 validates only texture/shape quantities (LV, HFE, ESSIM, GC), contains no grayscale or channel-shuffle rows, and supplies no color-preservation/suppression metric. It also does not quantify color changes caused by bilateral filtering or patch operations. Thus the assertion that the transformations selectively suppress all three feature types, particularly color, is unsupported by the presented validation.

CLIP does not inherently provide an ImageNet classifier in the same sense as the supervised timm models; its ImageNet classification normally requires a specified text encoder, prompt template(s), class-name mapping, and image-text logit computation, or a separately trained classification head. The manuscript merely says that checkpoints were obtained from timm and that predictions use argmax, while reporting a CLIP-ViT accuracy of 0.936. It never specifies the CLIP checkpoint variant or the zero-shot/head and prompt protocol, so this result is not reproducible and is not demonstrably comparable to the other models.

The paper reports a human-subject experiment involving twenty participants, masked 200-ms trials, attention checks, exclusions, and a forced-choice interface. It gives no statement of ethics/IRB review or exemption, informed consent, recruitment, compensation, participant eligibility, or data/privacy handling. The generic declaration that funders had no role does not address human-subject protections. These omissions require correction or an explicit statement that the applicable review and consent requirements were met.

Reference [41] is Wang et al.'s original SSIM paper, "Image quality assessment: from error visibility to structural similarity." It does not define an "Edge-SSIM" metric under the name ESSIM. The manuscript supplies neither a formula nor a separate source for its claimed edge-based variant. Since ESSIM is central to Table 2's validation and is used to justify the transformations, citing ordinary SSIM as though it establishes Edge-SSIM is an inadequate/misattributed metric definition.
